title: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Tool‑Augmented Agent vs LLM‑Only Generation for Intent‑Driven Network Configuration
abstract: We conducted a preregistered, paired, confirmatory study (n=300 tasks, 299 complete pairs) to test whether augmenting an LLM with a deterministic network verifier and a lightweight topology simulator (tool‑augmented agent) improves deterministic‑verifier pass rates and reduces simulated outage incidence versus an LLM‑only pipeline on synthetic intent‑to‑configuration NetOps tasks. The study used gpt-5-mini to generate candidate configurations from a shared initial generation semantics, a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and a paired binary analysis executor. Observed verifier‑pass rates were identical: baseline 299/299, guarded 299/299 (paired difference 0.00, McNemar two‑sided p=1.0; bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], 10k resamples). Because the preregistered execution used a shared initial candidate across conditions by design, the run is conclusive about the executed pipeline (no difference) but inconclusive about whether an independently generated tool‑augmented workflow would improve outcomes. We report the full preregistration, execution manifest, analysis artifacts, and deterministic hashes; discuss failure modes, construct and external‑validity threats, and practical next steps (independent per‑condition generation, multi‑model replication, richer simulators).

sections.introduction: Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into low‑level device configuration for network operations (NetOps). Prior work explores intent‑driven translation, verifier‑assisted repair, and tool‑augmented agent workflows to mitigate harmful or outage‑inducing misconfigurations [10.1002/nem.2313; arXiv:2403.09369; 10.5220/0013221900003890]. Research question and contribution. We preregistered and executed a paired experiment to answer: does augmenting an LLM with a deterministic network verifier and a topology‑aware simulator (the guarded agent) increase deterministic‑verifier pass rates versus an LLM‑only baseline on matched synthetic intent tasks? Our contribution is a fully preregistered, archived execution and analysis (study_id cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1) with machine‑readable artifacts and deterministic hashes, reporting exactly the observed outcomes and lessons for future confirmatory designs.
sections.related_work: LLM‑based intent translation and configuration automation have been studied across intent‑to‑config pipelines, fine‑tuning, and task‑specific approaches [Nguyen Tu et al., 2024 10.1002/nem.2313; PreConfig, arXiv:2403.09369]. Tool‑augmented and verifier‑assisted agent architectures are proposed to reduce hallucination and improve safety in agentic workflows [WeClaw 2026 10.2139/ssrn.7317098; Verifier Tax 2026 10.1145/3786335.3813160]. Benchmarks for groundedness and faithfulness motivate generate–validate–repair patterns but vary in task realism and validator strength. We situate our work as a tightly constrained, preregistered proof‑of‑execution that pairs tasks within‑subject to increase internal sensitivity and that instrumentally preserves full execution provenance.
sections.methodology: Preregistration. The complete preregistration (cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1) was frozen before execution and includes primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), sampling plan (300 paired tasks: 150 simple, 150 complex), power plan (targeted absolute improvement 0.20, n=300), and frozen analysis executors. Data and tasks. We used a public synthetic topology/template pool and a deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). Tasks specified initial and expected final states, allowed/touched fields, and workflow constraints (example patterns: shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break). Execution contract. Adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1; model provider openai_responses; model gpt-5-mini; maximum_model_calls 600. Generation semantics. The frozen contract specified shared_initial_candidate semantics (shared initial LLM generation reused across conditions) and maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1. Validator and simulator. Deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 checked command sequences against workflow constraints and produced a binary pass/fail verdict and structured validator traces. Analysis plan. Primary analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1: paired McNemar/bootstrapped paired CI (10k resamples, seed=1729). Sensitivity analyses and contamination detection (exact matches and token similarity thresholds) were predeclared. Execution and provenance. All model calls, raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, and artifact hashes were recorded; execution_manifest and analysis artifacts archived with SHA‑256 sums.
sections.results: Execution summary. Planned 600 episodes (300 pairs); completed 598 episodes (299 complete pairs); 2 failed episodes logged and retained in manifest. Model calls used: 300; model_configuration declared gpt-5-mini. Primary outcome. Deterministic validator pass counts: baseline successes 299/299, guarded successes 299/299 (complete_pair_count=299). Contingency: n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline)=0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p=1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI for paired difference = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Missingness and exclusions. One pair excluded from complete‑pair analysis due to dual technical failure; no confirmatory exclusions for contamination (exact matches/token similarity flags = 0). Secondary endpoints. Simulated outage indicators were collected as exploratory artifacts; no discordance between conditions was observed in the confirmatory set. Representative examples and validator traces. We include representative per‑task shared initial responses and validator traces (see artifact paths in the archived bundle).
sections.discussion: Interpretation. The executed pipeline produced identical verifier‑pass outcomes for both conditions; the confirmatory hypothesis of an absolute pass‑rate improvement was not supported. Crucially, the preregistered execution semantics used a shared_initial_candidate (single LLM generation reused across both baseline and guarded conditions). That design choice—recorded in the preregistration and execution manifest—means the run tests the downstream effect of verifier/tool intervention on a shared candidate rather than the effect of independently generated tool‑augmented outputs. In other words, the null result is a valid, verifiable outcome of the executed design but does not rule out benefits from a design in which the guarded agent issues independent generation or additional per‑condition model interactions. Lessons learned. (1) Shared‑candidate semantics reduce variance but can mask generation‑level improvements; independent per‑condition generation should be used when the research question asks whether tool‑augmentation changes the model’s produced artifact set. (2) Deterministic validators and rich simulator traces are valuable for traceability and for diagnosing failure modes. (3) Synthetic tasks enabled full determinism and provenance but limit external generalizability.
sections.conclusion: We reported a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired study comparing a tool‑augmented guarded pipeline to an LLM baseline on synthetic intent‑to‑configuration tasks. Observed verifier‑pass rates were identical in the executed design (299/299 each; paired difference 0.00, p=1.0), a conclusion that derives directly from the archived artifacts and analysis. Because the preregistered execution used a shared initial LLM candidate across conditions, the experiment is conclusive for the executed protocol but inconclusive for the broader question of whether tool‑augmentation improves outcomes when the agent is allowed independent generation or richer tool use. We release the preregistration, raw responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support replication. Future confirmatory work should preregister independent per‑condition generation, replicate across multiple LLMs, widen task diversity (including real operational logs), and examine trade‑offs in model calls and latency.

limitations: The preregistered execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (single LLM generation reused across baseline and guarded) by design; this constrains inference about independent tool‑augmented generation improvements.
Tasks were synthetic and simulator‑executed; external validity to real production devices and vendor CLIs is limited.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or sizes.
The deterministic validator and lightweight simulator approximate operational effects but cannot fully emulate complex runtime behaviour or inter-device side effects.

Because both conditions observed identical generated artifacts in this run, the study cannot adjudicate potential benefits of deeper tool invocation, iterative generation, or heterogeneous multi‑model orchestration.
